items.title: Contextual Needs Quiz
items.subtitle: Test your understanding of contextual spending priorities.

questions.prompt: Why is it dangerous to simply copy another person's personal budget template line by line?

options.text: Because their income, vocation, family dependencies, and living context are completely different from yours.
Because budgets are protected by copyright law.
Because only certified accountants are allowed to use templates.

questions.explanation: Your budget must reflect your individual reality, vocation, and specific constraints.

groups.title: When Your Money Cannot Cover Everything
groups.objective: Analyze financial rationing, emergency prioritization, and triage under scarcity.

items.title: The Medical Emergency Triage
items.subtitle: When an unexpected crisis forces immediate reallocation of all available cash.

scenario.narrative: Ngozi had budgeted ₦120,000 for the month: ₦50,000 for groceries, ₦30,000 for transport, ₦20,000 for savings, and ₦20,000 for a weekend wedding reception outfit. In week two, her elderly mother falls ill and requires an immediate ₦45,000 diagnostic medical scan. Ngozi has no emergency fund.

characters.name: Ngozi
characters.details: Facing unexpected medical emergency with fixed funds

prompts.prompt: How must Ngozi reallocate her budget to survive the month?

options.label: Cancel the wedding outfit, pause all non-essential spending, pay for the scan, and live on strict grocery staples.
Buy the wedding outfit anyway and ignore the hospital.
Take a 50% monthly loan app advance to buy the outfit.

items.debrief: Financial triage requires brutally honest prioritization. In emergencies, life and health immediately trump social appearances. Having an emergency fund prevents life events from destroying your monthly grocery runway.
items.key_takeaway: In financial emergencies, survival and health take 100% precedence over social desires.

items.title: The Financial Triage Hierarchy
items.subtitle: The four tiers of survival spending.

items: Tier 1 (Survival): Food, urgent medical care, basic shelter rent, basic utilities.
Tier 2 (Livelihood): Transport to work, tools required to generate daily income.
Tier 3 (Obligations): Minimum legal debt payments, insurance premiums.
Tier 4 (Discretionary): Entertainment, social clothing, dining out, luxury upgrades (cut 100% in a crisis).

items.title: Crisis Triage Allocator
items.subtitle: Allocate limited emergency funds across competing urgent demands.

items.title: Financial Triage Quiz
items.subtitle: Assess your ability to prioritize during unexpected emergencies.

questions.prompt: When facing a sudden severe income drop, which category of spending should be eliminated first?

options.text: Discretionary wants (dining out, entertainment, fashion, non-essential subscriptions)
Basic nutritional food for children
Life-saving prescription medications

questions.explanation: Discretionary spending should be completely eliminated first to preserve vital shelter, food, and health.

groups.title: Comparing Priorities and Ranking Goals
groups.objective: Learn how to rank competing financial objectives (e.g. debt repayment vs investing vs emergency fund).

items.title: The Three Competing Goals
items.subtitle: How to allocate a monthly surplus across debt, savings, and investments.

scenario.narrative: Emeka has a monthly surplus of ₦50,000 after covering all essential living expenses. He has three competing desires: 1) Repay a ₦200,000 loan app debt charging 15% monthly interest, 2) Build a ₦300,000 emergency fund (currently at ₦0), and 3) Invest in a stock market portfolio yielding 18% annually.

characters.name: Emeka
characters.details: Has ₦50,000 surplus; must rank order of financial operations

prompts.prompt: What is the mathematically and strategically correct order of priority for Emeka?

options.label: 1) Build a mini emergency buffer (₦50k), 2) Aggressively eradicate the 180% toxic loan debt, 3) Invest in stocks.
Invest 100% in stocks while letting the 180% loan app compound.
Spend the surplus on a luxury watch.

items.debrief: Financial priorities have a strict logical order of operations. Investing in the stock market to earn 18% a year while paying 180% annual interest on toxic loans is mathematical madness. Eradicate toxic debt first.
items.key_takeaway: Eliminate high-interest debt before deploying capital into long-term investments.

items.title: The Financial Order of Operations
items.subtitle: The universal sequence for deploying your financial surplus.

items: Step 1: Starter Emergency Fund (1 month of basic living expenses).
Step 2: Toxic Debt Eradication (Pay off all loans with interest above 15%).
Step 3: Fully Funded Emergency Shield (3 to 6 months of living expenses).
Step 4: Long-Term Compound Investing (Equities, real estate, productive assets).
Step 5: Major Lifestyle Goals (Home ownership, luxury travel, philanthropy).

items.title: Financial Priority Ranker
items.subtitle: Rank financial goals into the correct sequence of execution.

items.label: Aggressively pay off high-interest loan apps and credit debt
Consistently invest 20%+ in long-term productive assets

items.title: Priority Ranking Quiz
items.subtitle: Test your understanding of the financial order of operations.

questions.prompt: Why should you pay off a 30% interest loan before investing in stocks that yield 15%?

options.text: Because paying off a 30% debt gives you a guaranteed 30% risk-free return by avoiding interest, which beats an uncertain 15% stock yield.
Because stock investments are illegal if you owe debt.
Because banks will delete your stock account.

questions.explanation: Eliminating debt is mathematically equivalent to earning a risk-free return equal to the interest rate avoided.

groups.title: Making Trade-offs and Accepting Constraints
groups.objective: Synthesize the reality that saying YES to one financial goal means saying NO to another.

items.title: The Business Capital vs. Luxury Wedding Choice
items.subtitle: Choosing between a one-day celebration and long-term financial security.

scenario.narrative: Kunle and his fiancée have saved ₦6,000,000. Kunle's extended family pressures them to host a 600-guest luxury wedding reception costing ₦6,000,000. Kunle also has an opportunity to buy a commercial logistics franchise route that yields ₦350,000 net monthly profit. After serious discussion, the couple hosts an elegant, intimate ceremony for ₦1,200,000 and deploys the remaining ₦4,800,000 into the franchise. Three years later, the franchise income has fully funded their first home.

characters.name: Kunle & Fiancée
characters.details: Chose asset creation over transient social spectacle

characters.name: Extended Family
characters.details: Demanded lavish 600-guest wedding reception

prompts.prompt: What made the couple's decision a masterclass in financial trade-offs?

options.label: They sacrificed transient social validation for a cash-generating asset that provided long-term security.
They hated all their friends and family.
Weddings are prohibited by the central bank.

items.debrief: Every major financial decision involves a trade-off. Choosing to spend millions on an 8-hour party means giving up a business, a house down-payment, or children's education funds. Mature adults evaluate the trade-off and choose long-term freedom.
items.key_takeaway: Maturity means accepting constraints and prioritizing long-term assets over transient celebrations.

items.title: The Power of Conscious Trade-offs
items.subtitle: You can afford anything, but not everything.

body.text: Personal finance author Paula Pant noted: 'You can afford anything, but you cannot afford everything.'

items: Saying YES to a lavish luxury apartment means saying NO to saving for your own business.
Saying YES to driving a modest car means saying NO to monthly vehicle debt stress.
Make your trade-offs consciously, intentionally, and without regret.

items.title: Trade-off Evaluation Matrix
items.subtitle: Compare the long-term trade-offs of major life expenditures.

items.subtitle: Comprehensive assessment of needs, wants, and trade-offs.

questions.prompt: What is an economic trade-off?

options.text: A situational decision where giving up or diminishing one desirable choice is necessary to gain another preferred alternative.
A barter transaction involving only farm vegetables.
A trade agreement between two hostile countries.

questions.explanation: Trade-offs are the fundamental reality of managing limited resources across competing human desires.

lessons.title: Opportunity Cost: The Hidden Cost of Every Decision
lessons.subtitle: Master economics' most profound insight: the true cost of anything is what you give up to get it.

contents.title: Every Choice Has Another Side
contents.objective: Understand opportunity cost, identify the next-best alternative, and evaluate unseen trade-offs.

groups.title: The Meaning of Opportunity Cost
groups.objective: Define opportunity cost as the value of the foregone next-best alternative.

items.title: Study for the Exam or Work the Shift?
items.subtitle: How students trade immediate cash for long-term qualification earnings.

scenario.narrative: Tari is offered a weekend bartending shift that pays ₦25,000 cash. However, taking the shift means he will not study for his final university engineering examination on Monday morning. If he fails the exam, he must pay ₦80,000 for a retake semester and delay his graduation by six months. Tari must evaluate the real cost of that ₦25,000.

characters.name: Tari
characters.details: Weighing ₦25k immediate cash vs academic graduation

data.label: The Opportunity Cost
data.value: Graduating on time with top grades

prompts.prompt: What is the opportunity cost if Tari chooses to work the bartending shift?

options.label: His exam preparation time and the risk of delaying his engineering graduation and career.
Only the cost of his bus ticket to the bar.
Zero, because earning cash is always 100% positive.

items.debrief: The opportunity cost of an action is not what you pay; it is the value of the next-best alternative you surrender. Earning ₦25,000 while risking ₦80,000 in retake fees and six months of delayed career salary is an extraordinarily expensive trade.
items.key_takeaway: The real cost of any decision includes everything you give up to make it.

items.title: What Is Opportunity Cost?
items.subtitle: The most important concept in all of economic science.

body.text: The loss of potential gain from other alternatives when one alternative is chosen.

items: When you spend ₦50,000 on shoes: The true cost is not just the ₦50,000; it is the shares you could have bought that would have paid dividends for twenty years.
When you spend 4 hours scrolling social media: The true cost is the new language, skill, or business you could have built in those 4 hours.
Money and time are finite; choosing A always means rejecting B.

items.title: Identify the Next-Best Alternative
items.subtitle: Pinpoint the exact opportunity cost across common life decisions.

config.prompt: You have ₦100,000 cash. You can: Option A: Buy a luxury designer watch, Option B: Invest in an index fund yielding 18% annual return, Option C: Store physical cash in a jar. If you choose Option A, what is your opportunity cost?

options.label: Option B: The 18% annual compound investment growth you surrendered.
Option C: The glass jar.
Zero, because you have a beautiful watch.

config.follow_up_prompt: Why is the opportunity cost always the NEXT-BEST alternative, rather than all other alternatives combined?

items.title: Opportunity Cost Definition Quiz
items.subtitle: Test your grasp of opportunity cost fundamentals.

questions.prompt: What does an economist mean by 'opportunity cost'?

options.text: The value of the next-best alternative you must give up when making a choice.
The total amount of cash printed on a store receipt.
The price of advertising a job opportunity.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost measures the highest-value option foregone when choosing one path over another.

groups.title: The Next-Best Alternative
groups.objective: Learn to identify and rank competing options before spending capital.

items.title: The ₦500,000 Graduation Gift
items.subtitle: Evaluating three mutually exclusive uses of capital.

scenario.narrative: Upon graduating from university, Halima's uncle gifts her ₦500,000 cash. Halima considers three options: 1) A luxury celebratory party with friends (Cost: ₦500k), 2) Professional data science certification and a high-performance laptop (Cost: ₦500k), and 3) A commercial high-yield treasury deposit (Cost: ₦500k). Her next-best alternative to the laptop is the treasury deposit.

characters.name: Halima
characters.details: Evaluating three competing uses of ₦500,000 windfall

prompts.prompt: If Halima chooses Option 2 (Data Science Certification), what did she give up, and was it a smart trade-off?

options.label: She gave up the ₦90k annual treasury yield and party, but gained a career asset capable of earning millions annually.
She lost all her money forever.
She gave up nothing.

items.debrief: Whenever evaluating a financial choice, write down the top two alternatives. The decision is worthwhile only if the chosen path delivers superior long-term utility than the next-best alternative.
items.key_takeaway: Compare your chosen path against the next-best alternative to ensure you are maximizing value.

items.title: Ranking Alternatives
items.subtitle: The discipline of the comparative balance sheet.

body.text: Before deploying significant capital, list your options in rank order:

items: Rank 1: Chosen option.
Rank 2: Next-best alternative (Your Opportunity Cost).
Rank 3+: Other lesser alternatives.
Rule: Only proceed if Rank 1 clearly outperforms Rank 2 across a multi-year horizon.

items.title: Windfall Allocation Matrix
items.subtitle: Rank three competing uses of a ₦500,000 windfall.

items.title: Next-Best Alternative Quiz
items.subtitle: Assess your ability to identify the precise opportunity cost.

questions.prompt: A farmer can use a 2-acre plot of land to plant maize (projected profit: ₦800,000), cassava (projected profit: ₦650,000), or build a storage barn (saves ₦400,000 in rentals). If the farmer plants maize, what is the opportunity cost?

options.text: ₦650,000 (the profit from planting cassava, the next-best alternative)
₦1,050,000 (cassava plus the barn combined)

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is strictly the value of the single next-best alternative foregone (cassava profit: ₦650,000).

groups.title: Why the Cheapest Option Is Not Always the Best
groups.objective: Examine lifecycle costs, durability, and false economy.

items.title: The ₦4,000 Counterfeit Shoes vs. ₦20,000 Leather Boots
items.subtitle: How buying cheap goods repeatedly costs far more in the long run.

scenario.narrative: Chinedu needs sturdy shoes for work on construction sites. He buys cheap counterfeit sneakers for ₦4,000. Within six weeks, the soles split and the shoes disintegrate in the rain. Over two years, Chinedu buys eight pairs of cheap shoes, spending ₦32,000 in total and enduring constant foot pain. His coworker buys one pair of authentic safety leather boots for ₦20,000 that lasts four full years.

characters.name: Chinedu
characters.details: Spent ₦32,000 over 2 years on 8 pairs of failing shoes

characters.name: Coworker
characters.details: Spent ₦20,000 on 1 durable pair that lasts 4 years

prompts.prompt: What economic fallacy did Chinedu fall into?

options.label: The 'False Economy' trap: buying low-quality cheap goods that fail repeatedly costs more over time than buying quality once.
Shoes are illegal to wear on construction sites.
He became richer by buying 8 pairs.

items.debrief: Author Terry Pratchett coined the 'Boots Theory of Socioeconomic Unfairness': poor people often spend more money over their lifetimes on cheap, failing items than wealthy people spend on durable, high-quality items. Whenever possible, evaluate total lifecycle cost rather than upfront sticker price.
items.key_takeaway: True value is measured by cost per year of use, not the initial purchase tag.

items.title: Cost Per Use: The True Price Formula
items.subtitle: How smart buyers evaluate purchases.

body.text: Total Purchase Price divided by Total Number of Times the Item Is Used.
A ₦60,000 work laptop used 250 days a year for 3 years costs ₦80 per day of use. A ₦30,000 party outfit worn once costs ₦30,000 per use. The laptop is hundreds of times cheaper in real terms.

items.title: Cost Per Use Calculator
items.subtitle: Calculate the real cost per use of any major purchase.

config.title: Cost Per Use Calculator
config.formula_display: Cost Per Use = Purchase Price ÷ Expected Number of Uses

items.title: False Economy Quiz
items.subtitle: Assess your understanding of lifecycle costs.

questions.prompt: What is a 'false economy' in personal finance?

options.text: An action that seems to save money initially (like buying poor quality tools), but ultimately results in higher total costs and wasted time.
A country that uses fake paper money.
A bank account with zero balance.

questions.explanation: A false economy appears cheap upfront, but ends up costing far more in repairs, replacements, and headaches.

groups.title: Spending Now vs. Saving for Later
groups.objective: Evaluate intertemporal choice: how present spending sacrifices future compound wealth.

items.title: The ₦2,000 Daily Coffee Habit
items.subtitle: How small daily leaks compound into millions over a decade.

scenario.narrative: Dayo buys an upscale takeout specialty iced latte and pastry every morning before work for ₦2,500. He considers it a minor expense. Over 20 workdays a month, that equals ₦50,000 monthly, or ₦600,000 per year. If Dayo brewed coffee at home for ₦300 and invested the remaining ₦44,000 monthly into an index fund compounding at 15% annually, he would accumulate over ₦12,500,000 in ten years.

characters.name: Dayo
characters.details: Spends ₦50k/mo on takeout beverages without tracking

prompts.prompt: What is the true opportunity cost of Dayo's daily takeout beverage?

options.label: Over ₦12,500,000 in compound investment wealth that could have funded a home deposit or business.
Only the ₦2,500 note paid that morning.
Zero, because coffee is healthy.

items.debrief: Small recurring leaks are the enemy of wealth accumulation because they steal from the future power of compound interest. A ₦50,000 monthly habit is not just ₦50,000; it is millions of foregone future wealth.
items.key_takeaway: Recurring daily habits have massive compounded opportunity costs over decades.

items.title: The Multiplier Effect of Compounded Savings
items.subtitle: Every naira you save today is worth several naira tomorrow.

body.text: Whenever you consider a non-essential recurring luxury, multiply its annual cost by the Rule of 10:
Every ₦100,000 you invest annually at 15% return compounds to approximately ₦2,000,000 over 10 years, and over ₦10,000,000 over 20 years.

items.title: Recurring Habit Opportunity Cost Calculator
items.subtitle: See how much a small daily spending habit would grow to if invested over 10 years.

items.title: Intertemporal Choice Quiz
items.subtitle: Assess your understanding of time-shifted spending.

questions.prompt: Why do economists evaluate small daily recurring expenses differently from one-off purchases?

options.text: Because small recurring expenses accumulate continuously and deprive your future of massive compound investment growth.
Because banks charge extra fees on small purchases.
Because small expenses are tax-exempt.

questions.explanation: Compounding turns small monthly savings into vast sums of capital over multi-year horizons.

groups.title: Studying, Working, and Using Your Time
groups.objective: Analyze time as your most scarce and irreplaceable economic asset.

items.title: The 3-Hour Daily Traffic Commute
items.subtitle: How time spent in gridlock represents massive foregone human capital.

scenario.narrative: Bisi rents an apartment far outside the city for ₦400,000 per year, saving ₦300,000 compared to an apartment near her office (₦700,000/yr). However, her commute consumes three hours in traffic every day (60 hours a month) and costs ₦25,000 extra in monthly bus fares (₦300,000/yr). The ₦300,000 she thought she saved on rent is wiped out by transport fares, and she loses 720 hours every year in traffic that she could have used to freelance or sleep.

characters.name: Bisi
characters.details: Trading 720 hours of life yearly for an illusion of rent savings

prompts.prompt: What was the real opportunity cost of Bisi's distant apartment?

options.label: 720 hours of personal life, health, and potential freelance earning power sacrificed for zero net financial savings.
The apartment had no roof.
Bus drivers were friendly.

items.debrief: Money lost can be earned back; time lost is gone forever. Bisi thought she was saving money on rent, but after accounting for transport fares, she saved ₦0 and sacrificed 720 hours of life. Always factor the economic value of your time into living decisions.
items.key_takeaway: Your time has economic value. Never trade hundreds of hours to save negligible amounts of cash.

items.title: The Hourly Value of Your Time
items.subtitle: Why wasting 4 hours to save ₦500 is an economic disaster.

body.text: Calculate your effective hourly wage: Divide your monthly net income by the total hours you work each month.

items: If you earn ₦2,000 per hour, spending 3 hours in lines or across town to save ₦1,000 is an economic loss of ₦5,000.
Treat your time with the exact same respect, discipline, and budgeting that you apply to your money.

items.title: Hourly Value Estimator
items.subtitle: Calculate the real monetary value of your working hours.

config.title: Hourly Time Valuation Tool
config.formula_display: Hourly Value = Monthly Net Earnings ÷ Monthly Hours

items.title: Time Valuation Quiz
items.subtitle: Test your understanding of time opportunity costs.

questions.prompt: A freelance programmer who earns ₦5,000 per hour spends 4 hours washing their car by hand to save ₦1,500 at a professional car wash. What was the net economic outcome?

options.text: A net economic loss of ₦18,500 (surrendered ₦20,000 of productive coding time to save ₦1,500).
A massive profit of ₦20,000.
A tie with zero economic effect.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost = 4 hours × ₦5,000/hr = ₦20,000 foregone. Subtracting ₦1,500 saved leaves an ₦18,500 net loss.

groups.title: Business Decisions and Limited Resources
groups.objective: Apply opportunity cost to corporate capital allocation, inventory selection, and business hiring.

items.title: The Bakery's Oven vs. Delivery Van Dilemma
items.subtitle: How a business owner allocates scarce capital between production capacity and logistics.

scenario.narrative: Madame Joy owns a thriving commercial bakery with ₦3,000,000 in retained expansion capital. She can either: 1) Buy an automated industrial deck oven that triples bread baking capacity, generating an estimated ₦600,000 extra monthly net profit, or 2) Buy a branded delivery van that saves ₦150,000 monthly in hired transport fees. She can only afford one.

characters.name: Madame Joy
characters.details: Evaluating two productive capital equipment investments

data.label: Optimal Decision
data.value: Option 1 generates 4x higher return on capital

prompts.prompt: Which capital investment maximizes business wealth and growth?

options.label: Buying the industrial oven: it triples production and generates ₦600,000 monthly, easily funding delivery rentals.
Buying the van because it looks prestigious on the road.
Leaving the ₦3M uninvested in a checking account.

items.debrief: Business capital is strictly finite. The opportunity cost of buying the delivery van was the ₦600,000 monthly profit from tripling bread production. By choosing the highest-yielding asset, Madame Joy expands her business rapidly.
items.key_takeaway: Businesses must allocate scarce capital to the projects with the highest return on investment.

items.title: Capital Allocation in Business
items.subtitle: The chief duty of every entrepreneur and CEO.

body.text: In business, capital allocation is everything. Every naira invested in inventory line A is a naira that cannot be invested in inventory line B.

items: Measure Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) across all projects.
Ruthlessly eliminate slow-moving, low-margin inventory.
Concentrate capital where profit margins, customer demand, and cash velocity are highest.

items.title: Business Capital Allocation Matrix
items.subtitle: Compare competing business investments based on projected monthly yield.

items.title: Business Capital Quiz
items.subtitle: Assess your understanding of corporate capital allocation.

questions.prompt: What should guide a small business owner when deciding between two competing equipment purchases?

options.text: Which equipment generates the highest net return on investment (ROI) and fastest cash-flow payback.
Which equipment has the brightest paint color.
Which equipment is sold by a friend.

questions.explanation: Capital must flow to the investments that produce the highest economic productivity and cash return.

items.title: The Financial Master's Dilemma
items.subtitle: Synthesizing purchasing power, inflation, compound interest, and opportunity cost in a single life decision.

scenario.narrative: David is 26 years old and has built a 6-month emergency cash fund. He receives a ₦1,000,000 annual bonus. He analyzes three choices: Choice 1: Upgrade to a luxury sports sedan with a ₦1M down payment and ₦120,000 monthly financing debt for 3 years. Choice 2: Leave the ₦1,000,000 in a 0% checking account. Choice 3: Invest the ₦1,000,000 in a diversified index fund compounding at 18% annually.

characters.name: David
characters.details: Evaluating choices using the full Module 1 financial framework

data.label: Choice 1 (Car Debt)
data.value: -₦4.3M total cash spent on a depreciating asset

data.label: Choice 2 (Idle Cash)
data.value: Loses 25% purchasing power annually to inflation

data.label: Choice 3 (Compounding Asset)

Choice 2: Letting inflation slowly destroy idle cash.

items.debrief: David's scenario brings all of Module 1 together: Money is a tool; inflation destroys idle cash; debt multiplies fragility; and compound interest in productive assets creates generational wealth. By understanding opportunity cost, David secures his financial independence.
items.key_takeaway: Every financial decision is connected. Choose assets over liabilities, beat inflation, and let compounding build your freedom.

contents.title: What Comes In, What Goes Out

items.title: Your Balance Has a Backstory
items.subtitle: See why knowing your current balance does not explain where your money came from or where it went.

body.text: Your account balance is a snapshot, not the full story.
To understand your money, track the money that comes in and the money that goes out.
Income is money received. An expense is money spent or owed for goods, services, or obligations.

items.title: Money Enter, Money Comot
items.subtitle: Separate incoming money from spending so you can understand your cash flow.

body.text: Examples of money coming in: wages, business sales, allowances, gifts, and freelance payments.
Examples of money going out: transport, food, data, rent contributions, subscriptions, and debt repayments.
A cash-flow record helps show whether you are spending less than, equal to, or more than you receive.

items.title: Sort Am Correctly
items.subtitle: Practise classifying common transactions as money in or money out.

cards.label: Salary
cards.feedback: Wages are income received.

cards.label: Transport fare
cards.feedback: Spending on transport is an expense.

cards.label: Gift received
cards.feedback: Gifts are money received.

cards.label: Data subscription
cards.feedback: A recurring expense.

cards.label: Repayment

config.extra_feedback: Borrowing creates money available now but also creates an obligation to repay.

items.feedback: Feedback explains each classification and clarifies that borrowing creates money available now but also an obligation to repay.

items.title: In or Out?
items.subtitle: Check whether you can classify everyday financial transactions accurately.

questions.prompt: You receive ₦15,000 for designing a flyer.
questions.explanation: Payment received for work is income.

questions.prompt: You pay ₦2,000 for transport.
questions.explanation: Money spent on a service is an expense.

questions.prompt: You borrow ₦10,000 from a friend.
questions.explanation: Cash comes in, but a repayment obligation is also created - borrowed money is not income.

questions.explanation: A promise to pay is not cash received.

groups.title: Small Spending, Big Picture
groups.objective: Use a simple record to see where money goes.

items.title: Where Did the ₦500 Go?
items.subtitle: Notice how repeated small purchases can add up across a week or month.

body.text: One small purchase may feel unimportant, but repeated purchases can become a meaningful part of your spending.
For example, spending ₦500 every day for 20 days totals ₦10,000.
The goal is not to shame small treats. It is to make spending visible so you can choose deliberately.

items.subtitle: Use a fictional spending record to identify patterns without judging the person.

prompts.prompt: How much did he spend?
How much remains?
Which categories might he want to review?

items.debrief: Learners should identify patterns and trade-offs, not assume that every optional expense is automatically wrong.

items.title: A Record Beats Guesswork
items.subtitle: Learn why writing down transactions is more reliable than relying on memory.

body.text: A simple record can include date, item or purpose, amount, and category.
You can use a notebook, spreadsheet, or a trusted app. The tool matters less than keeping the record consistently.
Record enough information to make decisions, but protect private financial information.

items.notes: There is no single correct category to cut; the reasoning must fit the person's priorities.

items.title: Your App Says ₦40k - Now What?
items.subtitle: Understand why a balance must be considered alongside upcoming bills and obligations.

body.text: A person may have ₦40,000 available today but owe ₦15,000 for a bill tomorrow.
The balance alone does not show what portion is already needed for a commitment.
A financial snapshot asks what you have, what you owe, and what payments are coming soon.

items.title: Money You Have vs. Money Already Spoken For
items.subtitle: Separate money currently available from money you have committed to a specific purpose.

body.text: If ₦10,000 is set aside for rent, treating it as free spending money can cause a shortfall.
A planned amount is not necessarily a separate legal account; it can simply be a clear personal allocation.
Knowing your commitments helps you avoid accidentally spending money needed for essential payments.

items.subtitle: Calculate what remains after subtracting near-term commitments from available money.

inputs.label: Transport and food needed before payday

outputs.label: Not yet allocated to these listed needs

groups.objective: Build a simple picture of what you own and owe.

items.title: Your Money Story Has Two Sides
items.subtitle: Recognise that a financial position includes resources as well as obligations.

body.text: Something of value that a person owns or controls.
A debt or other financial obligation.
The value of assets minus liabilities. It is a snapshot and does not replace a cash-flow plan.

items.title: Two People, Same Salary
items.subtitle: Compare two fictional financial situations to see why income alone cannot describe financial health.

scenario.narrative: Scenario A: Ada earns ₦120,000 monthly, has ₦80,000 in savings, and owes ₦10,000. Scenario B: Bode earns ₦120,000 monthly, has ₦20,000 in savings, and owes ₦150,000.

prompts.prompt: Do they earn the same amount?
Are their current obligations the same?
What else would you need to know before judging their overall situation?

items.debrief: The figures show different snapshots, but a full assessment would also consider expenses, assets, repayment terms, dependants, and income stability.

contents.title: Build a Budget That Fits Real Life
contents.objective: Create a realistic plan for allocating expected income to needs, wants, commitments, and future priorities.

groups.title: Tell Every Naira Its Job
groups.objective: Create a realistic plan for allocating expected income.

items.title: A Budget Is a Plan, Not a Prison
items.subtitle: Understand a budget as a flexible plan for deciding what your money needs to do.

body.text: A budget estimates money coming in and assigns money to spending, saving, and obligations.
It helps you compare priorities before money disappears through unplanned purchases.
A useful budget should reflect real income, real costs, and reasonable flexibility.

items.title: Start with What Is Certain
items.subtitle: Build a budget around realistic income rather than money you merely hope to receive.

body.text: List reliable income first.
If income varies, use a cautious estimate based on what is reasonably likely, then adjust when money actually arrives.
Avoid making essential commitments based only on uncertain future income.

items.title: Budget Builder: Naija Edition
items.subtitle: Allocate a fictional monthly income across expenses and priorities.

validation_feedback: alignment with the learner's stated priorities

options.text: Yes, it fits exactly
Yes, with ₦5,000 left over

No, it exceeds income by ₦15,000

items.title: Your Budget Must Know Your Life
items.subtitle: Recognise that essential costs differ across people's circumstances.

body.text: A student living at home may have different costs from a student renting a room.
A person supporting family members may have obligations that another person does not.
A budget should be judged by whether it fits the person's actual circumstances, not by copying somebody else's spending plan.

prompts.prompt: Which obligations are time-sensitive?

items.debrief: Identify priorities, consider lower-cost alternatives, and avoid assuming every situation has an easy solution.

contents.title: When the Plan Meets Reality

groups.title: Life No Dey Follow Spreadsheet

items.subtitle: See why a budget needs room for changing costs and surprises.

items.title: Saving No Be Competition
items.subtitle: Recognise that a useful saving habit is about consistency and purpose, not comparing amounts with other people.

body.text: Setting aside some available money for future use rather than spending it now.
The amount that is realistic depends on income, essential costs, obligations, and circumstances.
A small, repeatable amount may be a better starting point than an ambitious target that cannot be maintained.

items.title: Give Tomorrow Something
items.subtitle: Connect saving today with a future expense or goal.

body.text: Saving can support planned purchases, education costs, future bills, or an emergency reserve.
A clear purpose makes it easier to decide how much to save and when the money may be used.
Savings should not be confused with money that must be spent on immediate essentials.

items.title: Pick a Realistic Starting Point
items.subtitle: Choose a saving amount that fits a fictional person's income and obligations.

config.scenario: A learner receives ₦20,000 monthly, contributes ₦12,000 to essential costs, spends ₦5,000 on transport and data, and has other small necessary costs. ₦3,000 remains before those other costs.

options.label: Save ₦500

options.risk: Progress toward a larger goal may be slower.

options.label: Save ₦1,000
options.benefit: Builds the habit faster than the smallest option.
options.tradeoff: Check whether the remaining amount is realistic.

options.label: Save ₦2,000

options.risk: Leaves only ₦1,000 before other necessary costs and may cause a shortfall.

body.text: A person may save separately for school materials, a device, a planned trip, or emergencies.

items.subtitle: Consider how an unplanned but necessary expense can disrupt a person's budget.

body.text: A phone needed for work suddenly needs repair.

items.title: Emergency, Need, or Want?
items.subtitle: Classify expenses by urgency and importance rather than by how strongly someone desires them.

body.text: An unexpected event requiring timely attention.
Something important for health, safety, basic living, or a significant obligation.
May be enjoyable or valuable but can often be delayed without serious harm.

questions.prompt: Essential medicine is needed today.

body.text: Borrowing may provide immediate funds, but it can add interest, fees, repayment dates, and pressure on future income.

lessons.title: Needs, Wants, and Impulse Spending

contents.title: Before You Tap Buy
contents.objective: Identify needs and wants, pause before impulse purchases, and assess a purchase against priorities.

groups.title: Want Am or Need Am?
groups.objective: Identify needs and wants and pause before impulse purchases.

items.title: Your Cart Is Not Your Priority List
items.subtitle: Separate what is necessary from what is desirable in a specific situation.

body.text: A need supports essential living, safety, health, work, or an important obligation.
A want can improve comfort or enjoyment but may be delayed or replaced.
The same item can be a need in one situation and a want in another.

items.title: One Budget, Four Choices
items.subtitle: Rank a fictional set of expenses according to urgency and personal circumstances.

scenario.narrative: A learner has ₦12,000. Choices include food for the next few days, transport to work, a phone case, and a new game.

choices: Food for the next few days

prompts.prompt: Rank the four choices and explain your ranking.
What extra information might change it?

items.debrief: The exercise is about reasoning and context, not labelling every enjoyable purchase as bad.

items.title: The Real Cost Is More Than the Price
items.subtitle: Consider what a purchase uses up besides the money paid at checkout.

body.text: A purchase also uses money that could have gone toward another goal.
Recurring payments can continue after the excitement of the first purchase fades.
Check total cost, maintenance, delivery, fees, and future commitments where relevant.

items.title: The 24-Hour Pause
items.subtitle: Practise delaying non-urgent purchases long enough to reconsider them.

config.setup: A tempting non-essential purchase is shown.
after_pause_questions: Can I afford it without missing a priority?
config.note: The pause is a decision aid, not a rule that must apply to every purchase.

items.feedback: Reveal what the learner's choice led to after a simulated pause.

groups.title: When Your Mood Holds Your Wallet
groups.objective: Recognise emotional triggers and build a personal pause rule.

items.title: Shopping to Change Your Mood
items.subtitle: Notice how boredom, stress, excitement, or disappointment can influence spending.

body.text: People sometimes spend to seek comfort, celebrate, fit in, or escape an unpleasant feeling.
The emotion is real, but a purchase may not solve the underlying problem.
Noticing the trigger creates a chance to choose a response deliberately.

items.title: The Bad-Day Checkout
items.subtitle: Help a fictional learner identify an emotional spending trigger and choose an alternative response.

scenario.narrative: After a stressful day, Sola orders expensive food and buys clothes online even though rent contribution is due.

prompts.prompt: What might have triggered the spending?
Which obligation is affected?
What alternative could Sola try before purchasing?

items.debrief: Suggestions may include a short break, talking to someone, choosing a lower-cost treat, or revisiting the budget after emotions settle.

items.title: Create Your Pause Rule
items.subtitle: Write a simple personal rule for reviewing purchases that are large, emotional, or non-essential.
items.task: Choose a threshold or situation that triggers a pause, list three checks (affordability, priority, total cost), and decide what to do if a check fails.

rubric.description: Affordability, priority and total cost included
States what happens if the purchase fails a check

contents.title: Social Pressure, Deals, and FOMO
contents.objective: Recognise social influence and marketing tactics that can push learners toward unplanned spending.

groups.title: Everybody Is Buying It
groups.objective: Separate personal goals from social pressure.

items.title: Their Lifestyle, Your Wallet
items.subtitle: Recognise how friends and social media can distort spending expectations.

body.text: Posts often show purchases and experiences without showing debt, income, family support, or trade-offs.
Copying someone else's lifestyle without knowing their financial situation can create pressure.
A useful decision is one that fits your priorities and resources, not one that proves you can keep up.

items.title: Whose Goal Is This?
items.subtitle: Identify whether a spending decision reflects a personal goal or external pressure.

questions.prompt: You save for a laptop required for your course.
categories: Personal goal linked to a need
questions.correct: Personal goal linked to a need
questions.explanation: The purchase serves your own need.

questions.prompt: You buy expensive shoes only because friends may mock your old ones.
categories: Personal goal linked to a need
questions.explanation: The motive is external approval.

questions.prompt: You compare prices and decide an item fits your plan.
categories: Personal goal linked to a need
questions.explanation: Comparison against your plan shows deliberate choice.

groups.title: Discount No Mean Free
groups.objective: Evaluate deals and time-limited offers.

items.title: You Saved ₦5,000 - Or Did You?
items.subtitle: Understand why a discount only saves money when the purchase itself makes sense.

body.text: If an item falls from ₦20,000 to ₦15,000, you pay ₦15,000 - you do not receive ₦5,000.
If you did not need the item or cannot afford it, the discount may still lead to unnecessary spending.
Compare the final price with your budget and alternatives, not just the size of the advertised discount.

items.title: The Flash Sale Trap
items.subtitle: Evaluate a time-limited offer without allowing urgency to replace affordability checks.

scenario.narrative: A learner sees headphones discounted from ₦30,000 to ₦22,000. They have ₦25,000 but need ₦18,000 for transport and food before payday.

prompts.prompt: Can the learner pay for the headphones and cover the listed essentials?
What would remain after paying for the headphones?
Is the discount enough reason to buy?

items.debrief: The discounted item is unaffordable within the stated constraints, even though the sale looks attractive.

items.title: Read the Small Print
items.subtitle: Check recurring charges, delivery fees, warranties, and conditions before committing to a purchase.

body.text: A low headline price may exclude delivery, service charges, or required accessories.
Subscriptions can renew automatically, creating future costs.
Before paying, check the total amount, cancellation terms, and whether the seller or service is legitimate.

items.title: Beat the FOMO Clock
items.subtitle: Use a short checklist to decide whether to buy, delay, or walk away from a tempting offer.
items.task: Answer: Do I need or genuinely want it? Can I afford it after essentials? Have I checked the full cost? Would I still buy it without the countdown timer? Then choose buy, delay, or walk away.

rubric.description: Chooses buy, delay, or walk away
Reasoning uses numbers and stated constraints

items.notes: The app rewards evidence-based reasoning, not automatically rejecting every purchase.

lessons.title: Set Financial Goals You Can Actually Reach

contents.title: Turn a Wish into a Plan
contents.objective: Convert vague financial wishes into specific targets with amounts, deadlines, and practical next steps.

groups.title: Wish, Goal, Plan
groups.objective: Convert vague wishes into measurable goals.

items.title: I Want to Save More Is Not a Plan
items.subtitle: Turn a broad intention into a goal that can be measured and acted on.

body.text: Something you would like to happen.
Identifies what you want to achieve, how much it costs, and when you want to achieve it.
Identifies the actions and contributions needed to move toward the target.

items.title: Give the Goal a Number and a Date
items.subtitle: Make a goal specific enough to calculate the amount and time required.

body.text: Example: Save ₦60,000 for a course fee in six months.
If no savings have been set aside, the simple average contribution required is ₦10,000 per month, before considering any fees or changes in cost.
If that amount does not fit the budget, reconsider the deadline, target, or ways to increase available funds.

items.title: Goal Calculator
items.subtitle: Calculate a simple regular contribution needed to reach a target by a chosen date.

config.validation: Flag unrealistic inputs (months <= 0, current > target) and remind that costs, income and timing can change.

items.feedback: Reminds learners that costs, income, and timing can change.

items.title: Goal or Just Vibes?
items.subtitle: Identify which statements contain a measurable financial goal.

questions.prompt: 'I want to be better with money.'
questions.explanation: No amount, deadline or action.

questions.prompt: 'I will save ₦30,000 for textbooks over three months.'
questions.explanation: Has an amount, purpose and deadline.

questions.prompt: 'I will save something someday.'
questions.explanation: No amount and no date.

groups.title: Put the Goals in Order
groups.objective: Order competing goals realistically.

items.title: Not Every Goal Comes First
items.subtitle: Prioritise goals by urgency, importance, cost, and consequences of delay.

body.text: People often have several goals but limited money.
A near-term essential payment may need priority over a discretionary purchase.
Priorities can change when income, responsibilities, or circumstances change.

items.title: The Laptop, the Rent, and the Trip
items.subtitle: Balance several competing goals and explain the consequences of the chosen order.

scenario.narrative: A learner wants to save for a laptop needed for coursework, contribute to rent by a deadline, and take a leisure trip.

prompts.prompt: Rank the goals using urgency, consequences, and available alternatives.

items.debrief: There may be more than one defensible plan, but essential commitments and deadlines must be considered explicitly.

items.title: Build Your Three-Goal Ladder
items.subtitle: Choose three fictional goals and create a realistic order for working toward them.
items.task: For each goal record target amount, deadline, priority, and next action. Explain which goal comes first and what you will do if the budget cannot fund all three at once.

rubric.description: Target, deadline, priority and next action for each goal
Explains why the first goal comes first
Plan if budget cannot fund all three

contents.title: Track Progress Without Giving Up
contents.objective: Monitor progress, respond to setbacks, and revise financial goals when circumstances change.

groups.title: Progress Is Data
groups.objective: Monitor progress and revise goals when circumstances change.

items.title: Small Steps Still Move You
items.subtitle: Use regular progress checks to see whether your plan is working.

body.text: Record how much you have saved and how much remains.
Compare actual contributions with the planned amount.
A slow month does not automatically mean failure; it gives you information to review the plan.

items.title: Progress Tracker
items.subtitle: Update a goal after each contribution and see how the remaining target changes.
items.feedback: Shows progress as both an amount and a proportion of the goal.

items.title: When the Plan Slips
items.subtitle: Revise a goal constructively when income, costs, or deadlines change.

body.text: Possible responses include changing the contribution amount, extending the deadline, reducing the target, or finding a realistic additional source of income.
Do not rely on risky borrowing or unrealistic promises just to preserve an old deadline.
A revised plan is useful when it reflects reality and keeps important priorities protected.

items.title: The Price Went Up
items.subtitle: Adjust a savings goal after the cost of the intended purchase increases.

scenario.narrative: A laptop originally expected to cost ₦180,000 now costs ₦210,000. The learner has saved ₦90,000 and has three months remaining.

prompts.prompt: How much more is needed?
What is the simple monthly contribution required if the deadline stays the same?

items.debrief: Decide whether that contribution is realistic and consider changing the deadline, target, or purchase option if necessary.

items.title: The Honest Goal Review
items.subtitle: Review a goal using actual progress and make one evidence-based adjustment.
items.task: Compare target progress with actual progress, identify the reason for any gap, choose one adjustment, and say how you will check whether it works.

rubric.description: Explains how it will be verified

final_quiz.title: Future You Is Counting on You
final_quiz.subtitle: Demonstrate that you can set a measurable goal, calculate contributions, and adapt when circumstances change.

questions.prompt: What makes a financial goal measurable?
questions.model_answer: A clear target and a way to track progress, usually including an amount and deadline.

questions.prompt: A learner needs ₦24,000 in four months and has nothing saved. What simple monthly contribution is required?
A goal becomes unaffordable after an unexpected cost. Name one reasonable response.
questions.model_answer: Revise the amount, timeline, target, or realistic income plan.

questions.prompt: Why should goals be prioritised?
questions.model_answer: Resources are limited and deadlines or consequences differ.

questions.prompt: Missing one contribution automatically means the goal has failed.
questions.explanation: Review the reason and adjust the plan.

evaluation_track.overview: The Evaluation Track measures learner performance across the Learning Track. It is derived from the `assessed: true` nodes (quizzes, challenges, capstone), their concept tags, and the lesson-level goals in each lesson.evaluation block.
evaluation_track.status_note: The syllabus defines WHAT is assessed (quiz at every Group, final quiz per Content, lesson challenges, capstone). Numeric thresholds, weights and formulas below are PROPOSED defaults so the developer has something concrete to build; product/learning team should tune them.

group_quiz.purpose: Check understanding right after the Group

practice_quiz.purpose: Reinforce difficult/misunderstood ideas (High and Very High lessons)

content_final.purpose: Test the whole Content unit; application over recall

lesson_assessment.purpose: Integrated lesson-level task (recommended for High/Very High)

module_capstone.purpose: Combine concepts across the module in one scenario

scoring.auto_graded: single_choice, true_false, numeric, classify -> 1.0 if correct else 0.0 (times question.points)
scoring.rubric_graded: challenge and short_answer: each rubric criterion scored 0-3; score = sum / (3 * criteria_count)
scoring.short_answer_default: key_points coverage ratio; >= 0.67 counts as correct, else partial credit = ratio
scoring.retries: Unlimited retries; first-attempt score is stored separately from best score.
scoring.feedback: Always show question.explanation after each answer (design rule: explanatory feedback, not just correct/wrong).

pass_and_gating.unlock_rule: Next Group unlocks when current Group's items are complete (quiz attempted). Next Content unlocks when the previous Content final quiz is >= content_final_pass. Learners may retry to improve.
pass_and_gating.remediation: If a group quiz score < pass: suggest replaying the relevant slides (by concept tags) and, in High/Very High lessons, offer the practice_quizzes. Practice quizzes never block progress.

mastery_model.unit: concept (ids in glossary.concepts and the `concepts` arrays on slides/widgets/questions)
mastery_model.formula: mastery(concept) = sum(w_a * s_q) / sum(w_a) over the learner's most recent N=8 scored responses tagged with the concept; w_a is the assessment_type weight; s_q in [0,1]
mastery_model.lesson_mastery: weighted mean of mastery over the lesson's concepts, weights = number of tagged questions

goals_and_tasks.goal: A lesson learning goal (lesson.evaluation.goals[]). Each goal links to the assessments that evidence it and has a mastery_threshold. goal_progress = (best weighted score across linked assessments) / threshold, capped at 1.
goals_and_tasks.task: A challenge, lesson_assessment or the Module capstone. Task completion = rubric_score >= challenge_pass. Rubric criteria give the learner specific, actionable feedback.
goals_and_tasks.learner_view: GoalsAndTasksBoard lists each goal with progress bar, each task with status (not started / submitted / passed), and the next recommended item.

concepts.definition: The direct exchange of goods or services for other goods or services without using money as an intermediary.
A situation in a barter system where two trade partners must each desire exactly what the other person is offering for a trade to occur.
An officially accepted instrument or currency used to facilitate the sale, purchase, or trade of goods and services.
A standard numerical monetary unit used to measure, record, and compare the market value of goods, services, and debts.
An asset or currency that reliably maintains its purchasing power into the future without rapidly deteriorating.
Currency issued and backed by government declaration and public trust, rather than backed by a physical commodity such as gold or silver.
Money whose value comes from the intrinsic physical worth of the commodity it is made of, such as gold coins, silver, or cowrie shells.
Any official currency declared by law that a creditor or merchant is legally obligated to accept in settlement of a financial debt.
Money received on a regular or periodic basis from work, capital investments, business sales, or gifts.
Money received in direct compensation for personal labor or professional services provided, including salaries, wages, tips, and commissions.
Earnings derived from an enterprise or asset in which an individual is not actively or continuously involved, such as rental income, dividends, or interest.
Any resource or item of economic value owned by an individual or company that can be converted into cash or generates future economic benefits.
An asset whose market value is expected to increase over time due to economic factors, growth, or demand (such as certain real estate or profitable equities).
An asset that loses market value over time due to physical wear, tear, age, or technological obsolescence (such as consumer electronics or motor vehicles).
A financial debt, legal obligation, or monetary amount owed by an individual or business to another entity.
The total financial value of everything an individual owns (assets) minus everything they owe (liabilities).
The net amount of cash and cash-equivalents being transferred into and out of an individual's or business's accounts over a specific period.
The ease and speed with which an asset or investment can be converted directly into cash without causing a significant drop in its market price.
The quantity and quality of goods or services that a single unit of currency can buy at any given point in time.
A general and sustained increase in the prices of goods and services across an economy over time, resulting in a reduction in purchasing power.
Extremely rapid and out-of-control inflation, typically exceeding 50% per month, which rapidly erodes the real value of the local currency.
A comprehensive economic index that measures the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of consumer goods and services.
The stated or face value of money, wages, or financial assets, unadjusted for the effects of inflation.
The value of money, wages, or assets adjusted for inflation, reflecting true purchasing power in terms of tangible goods and services.
The price at which one national currency can be converted into or exchanged for another national currency.
A fall in the value of a currency in a floating exchange rate system relative to foreign currencies, making imports more expensive.
Assets held on reserve by a central bank or monetary authority in foreign currencies to back liabilities, maintain currency stability, and pay foreign trade obligations.
The complex system of production, distribution, trade, and consumption of goods and services by different agents in a given geographic area.
The total monetary or market value of all finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period.
The economic principle stating that the price of a good or service is determined by the balance between consumer demand and producer supply in the marketplace.
The market price at which the quantity of a product demanded by consumers equals the quantity supplied by producers.
The fundamental economic problem of having unlimited human wants in a world of limited resources.
The percentage amount charged by a lender to a borrower for the use of assets, or paid by a bank to a depositor for holding funds.
Interest calculated on both the initial principal amount and all accumulated interest from previous periods, leading to exponential growth over time.
An independent national financial institution responsible for overseeing monetary policy, currency issuance, interest rate benchmarks, and banking supervision.
A significant and widespread decline in economic activity lasting for an extended period, commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth.
The percentage of the total labor force that is jobless and actively seeking employment.
A systematic pattern of deviation from rationality in financial judgment and decision-making due to cognitive shortcuts or emotional influences.
The human tendency to heavily discount future payoffs and overvalue immediate gratification, leading to undersaving and impulse spending.
A psychological phenomenon where the psychological pain of losing an amount of money is felt approximately twice as intensely as the pleasure of gaining an equal amount.
The cognitive tendency to disproportionately rely on the first piece of information encountered (the 'anchor') when making subsequent financial estimates or decisions.
The psychological tendency for individuals in a financial group or market to imitate the actions and spending choices of the majority rather than conducting independent analysis.
The irrational tendency to continue pouring money, time, or energy into a losing commitment simply because of prior unrecoverable investments.
The habit of increasing spending, luxuries, and recurring expenses in lockstep with every increase in income, preventing wealth accumulation.
Spending money on luxury goods and services primarily for the public display of income or social status rather than practical utility.
The distinction between essential expenses required for survival and basic functioning versus discretionary desires that enhance comfort or pleasure.
Non-essential expenditures on goods and services that a consumer chooses to purchase only if they have sufficient funds after paying for basic living expenses.
Mandatory living costs that are strictly necessary to maintain health, safety, shelter, and basic employment (such as rent, basic groceries, healthcare, and utilities).
The potential financial or lifestyle benefit that is foregone when choosing one alternative over the next-best available alternative.
A situational decision that involves giving up or sacrificing one valuable aspect or choice in order to gain another desirable advantage.
A forward-looking financial plan that estimates income and systematically allocates expenses over a defined period.
A dedicated cash reserve set aside in a secure, liquid account to cover unforeseen financial emergencies such as job loss, medical expenses, or urgent repairs.
A specific, measurable target an individual strives to reach with their money over a defined timeline, such as saving for education or buying property.
The capacity of an individual or household to withstand, adapt to, and recover from unexpected adverse financial events and economic shocks.
